The most important was Baudelaire, the writer of Les Fleurs du mal (The Flowers of Evil). Another model was Théodore de Banville, who taught Verlaine to enjoy clever rhymes and short lines. Verlaine also learned from Leconte de Lisle, one of the main Parnassian poets. He also loved the paintings of Antoine Watteau. Watteau's gentle scenes from the 18th century later helped to shape one of Verlaine's books. Verlaine's father died in December 1865. It was a very sad year for him. In 1866, Verlaine published his first book of poems, Poèmes saturniens (Saturnine Poems). The title comes from the planet Saturn. In an old belief, people born "under Saturn" were thought to be unlucky and sad. The book begins with a poem which says that such people must suffer and cannot escape their fate. In this first book, Verlaine uses strange and unusual names and shows his skill with rich rhymes. He wanted to prove that a poet must work hard on the craft of poetry. However, the book also contains real sadness. Some of its poems are among his best-loved works, including "Chanson d'automne" and "Mon rêve familier". One group of poems is called "Paysages tristes" ("Sad Landscapes"). In these poems, the light slowly changes from day to night while the feeling becomes sadder. This first book already showed Verlaine's special gift for making poetry sound like music. In February 1867, Élisa Moncomble died. She was now married and was known as Élisa Dujardin. Verlaine had loved her since he was a young child, and her death hurt him deeply. He remained drunk for three days. Some writers about his life have connected several of his early love poems with her. At the end of the same year, Verlaine published a small book of poems called Les Amies (The Women Friends). The poems were about love between women. Verlaine used a false name and had the book printed in Brussels. In 1868, however, a French court ordered the book to be destroyed and made the publisher pay a fine. In 1869, Verlaine published his next book, Fêtes galantes (Gallant Parties). The book was inspired by the paintings of Watteau. It shows elegant people in beautiful gardens in the style of the 18th century. They play music, flirt, and wear masks. However, beneath the beautiful surface, the poems often feel sad and unreal. The famous poem "Clair de lune" opens the book. Many readers see Fêtes galantes as one of Verlaine's finest works. During these years, Verlaine's drinking became worse. When he was drunk, he could be cruel. A letter written in July 1869 by a young woman from the Ardennes describes his heavy drinking and his violence towards his mother during a stay in the countryside. It shows that his behaviour had already become a serious problem. In June 1869, Verlaine met a young woman named Mathilde Mauté. She was the half-sister of his friend Charles de Sivry. Verlaine fell in love with her, and they became engaged in October. He hoped that a quiet married life would help him become calmer and more responsible. While they were engaged, Verlaine wrote a book of love poems for Mathilde called La Bonne Chanson (The Good Song). The poems are gentle, simple, and full of hope. He completed the book early in 1870, but it did not appear in bookshops until 1872 because of the war and other problems. Paul and Mathilde married on 11 August 1870. Mathilde had been born in April 1853, so she was only seventeen years old. Soon after the wedding, France went to war against Prussia, a German state, in the Franco-Prussian War. France lost the war. The French Empire fell, and a new republic was declared. The German army surrounded Paris during a long siege. During this time, Verlaine served in the National Guard, a force of ordinary citizens who helped to defend the city. In March 1871, a new city government called the Paris Commune took control of Paris. It wanted major political and social changes and opposed the national government. Verlaine supported it. He kept his office job and worked in the press office at the city hall, where he helped to deal with news and public information. After a few weeks, the national army from Versailles defeated the Commune during a very bloody week in which many people were killed. After the fall of the Commune, Verlaine lost his job. In September 1871, a young poet from the countryside sent letters and poems to Verlaine. His name was Arthur Rimbaud. He was not yet seventeen years old, but he was already writing powerful and unusual poems. Verlaine invited him to Paris. Rimbaud arrived on 10 September 1871 and stayed for a time in the house where Verlaine lived with his wife and her parents. Verlaine's son, Georges, was born a few weeks later, on 30 October 1871. He was Verlaine's only child. The two poets became very close, and their friendship soon became a love affair. This caused great pain in Verlaine's home. Mathilde became jealous and unhappy, while Verlaine became more violent towards her. He drank more and often stayed away from home. Rimbaud and Verlaine were very different people, and they often argued. Some of their arguments became violent. Their relationship was strong but unstable. The letters and other accounts that still exist do not show exactly what each man felt. On 7 July 1872, Verlaine left his wife and son. He and Rimbaud travelled together, first to Belgium and then to London. In London, they spent time with other French people who had left France after the Commune. Mathilde tried to persuade her husband to return to Paris, but she failed. She then began legal action to separate from him. During this period of travel, Verlaine wrote a new book of poems called Romances sans paroles (Songs Without Words). Many readers believe that it is his greatest book. The poems are very free and musical. Some describe grey and rainy days or quiet and sad rooms. Others describe towns in Belgium and England. The famous poem "Il pleure dans mon cœur" comes from this book. In the poem, rain falling on the town becomes an image of sadness that has no clear cause. Rimbaud also wrote Une saison en enfer (A Season in Hell) around this time. Part of the book looks back on the pain and arguments of their life together, although it also deals with many other subjects. By 1873, the two poets were arguing often, and Rimbaud wanted to leave. On 3 July, after a serious argument in London, Verlaine suddenly travelled to Brussels. Rimbaud followed him there. On the morning of 10 July 1873, Verlaine was drunk. He bought a gun and fired two shots at Rimbaud. One bullet struck Rimbaud in the wrist and wounded him, but the injury was not deadly. At first, the situation seemed to become calmer, and a doctor treated Rimbaud's arm. Later that day, however, Verlaine frightened Rimbaud again with the gun while they were in the street. Rimbaud became afraid and asked a police officer for help. Verlaine was arrested on the same day. Verlaine was put on trial for shooting and wounding Rimbaud. However, other facts were also used against him. The police had found letters about the love affair between the two men. At that time, many people strongly disapproved of such a relationship. The authorities also knew that Verlaine had worked for the Paris Commune. On 8 August 1873, he was sentenced to two years in prison and had to pay a fine. At first, he was held in the Petits-Carmes prison in Brussels. Prison life was hard and lonely. His head was shaved, he had to wear prison clothes, and he spent his days sorting coffee beans. In one of his letters, he wrote that this work "kills time". On 25 October 1873, he was moved to the prison at Mons, where he spent the rest of his sentence. After some time, he was allowed to read and study. He worked on his English and Spanish. Verlaine began writing again while he was in prison. He collected these prison poems for a book that he planned to call Cellulairement, which means roughly "In My Cell". However, he never published it as a separate book. Instead, he later placed its poems in several other collections. While Verlaine was in prison, his friend Lepelletier arranged for Romances sans paroles to be published in 1874. Verlaine also began writing many of the poems that later appeared in Sagesse (Wisdom). On 24 April 1874, a court in Paris made his separation from Mathilde official. It also decided that Georges would live with his mother. This news caused Verlaine great pain. While he was in prison, Verlaine returned to the Catholic faith. He had grown up in a Catholic family but had stopped believing when he was a young man. After he learned about the legal separation from Mathilde, he asked the prison chaplain, the priest who worked in the prison, for a book about the Catholic faith. He read it and was deeply moved. In June 1874, he told the chaplain that he now believed. Later that year, he received Communion again. People have disagreed about how deep and honest this change was. Some of his friends did not believe that it was real, while others said that his faith was sincere and strong. Biographers also disagree about what caused him to return to religion. However, faith became one of the main subjects of Verlaine's later poetry. His book Sagesse, which is full of prayers and religious feeling, is often considered one of his finest works. Verlaine was released from prison on 16 January 1875. At the end of February, he met Rimbaud for the last time in Stuttgart, Germany. The meeting ended in an argument, and the two poets never worked together again. Before they separated, Rimbaud gave Verlaine the manuscript of his prose poems, Illuminations. He asked Verlaine to send it to someone who could publish it. Rimbaud later stopped writing poetry and left Europe. Verlaine needed to earn money, so he went to England and worked as a teacher. He taught French, drawing, and other subjects in small towns such as Stickney, Boston, and Bournemouth. While he was in London, he also met another young poet, Germain Nouveau. Verlaine later returned to France. From 1877, he taught at a school in Rethel, in the Ardennes. There, he became very close to one of his pupils, a young man named Lucien Létinois. Verlaine described their relationship as that of a father and son, but writers about his life do not agree about its exact nature. In 1879, Verlaine took Lucien Létinois to England, where he again found work as a teacher. In 1880, Verlaine's mother gave money to buy a farm at Juniville, in the Ardennes, for the Létinois family. Verlaine lived there with them. In the same year, his book Sagesse was published. At first, however, very few people bought it. The farm soon had serious money problems and failed early in 1882. In April 1883, Lucien Létinois died of typhoid fever. Verlaine was again overcome by grief. He later wrote poems in memory of the young man in his book Amour (Love). After Lucien's death, Verlaine's mother bought another farm called Malval, at Coulommes. Verlaine went to live there with her. However, he could not continue a quiet life in the countryside. His drinking and money problems soon returned. In 1882, Verlaine returned to Paris and again became part of the literary world. His name slowly became better known. In 1884, he published two important books. The first was a book of essays called Les Poètes maudits (The Cursed Poets). In it, he praised several poets who were not well known at the time, including Rimbaud, Stéphane Mallarmé, and Tristan Corbière. The book helped more readers discover their work. The second book was Jadis et Naguère (Long Ago and Not Long Ago). It includes his famous poem "Art poétique", in which he explains some of his ideas about how poetry should be written. Verlaine's private life remained difficult. Mathilde received a full divorce in February 1885, after divorce had again become legal in France. Around the same time, Verlaine was accused of threatening his mother during a drunken argument. He was tried at Vouziers and spent about one month in prison. His health was also becoming worse. He had a serious problem with his knee and often had to stay in hospital. His mother died in January 1886. In the same year, he met a young artist named Frédéric-Auguste Cazals. Verlaine felt a strong love for him, but Cazals did not fully return it. The late 1880s were the worst years of Verlaine's poverty. He had almost no money and moved between cheap rooms and hospitals. In 1887, he was extremely poor and nearly died. Other writers helped him by giving him money. One of them was the poet François Coppée. From 1888, people often saw a strange sight in the Latin Quarter of Paris, near the university. Verlaine walked slowly through the streets, tapping the ground with his walking stick. He limped because of his bad leg, and a group of young poets often followed him. He spent many hours in cafés and much time at the Broussais hospital, where he continued to write. His hospital room sometimes became a meeting place where young poets came to visit him. During his last years, Verlaine met two women, Philomène Boudin and Eugénie Krantz. Both had worked as prostitutes. Each woman became his companion at different times, and they were rivals. Verlaine lived with Eugénie Krantz at the end of his life. Although he was poor and ill, Verlaine continued to write and publish. He brought out more books of poetry, including Amour (1888), Parallèlement (1889), Bonheur (Happiness, 1891), and Chansons pour elle (Songs for Her, 1891). He wrote religious poems in Liturgies intimes (1892), as well as prose books about his life and his stays in hospital. He also wrote private poems about love between men and love between women. A few of these poems were published in secret, and one book, Hombres, was published only after his death. In 1892 and 1893, he travelled to give public talks in the Netherlands, Belgium, England, and France. By the early 1890s, Verlaine was famous. In 1894, after the death of Leconte de Lisle, a magazine held a vote among writers to choose a new "Prince of Poets". Verlaine won the vote. He also tried to become a member of the Académie française, the famous group of leading French writers. However, he did not make the usual visits to its members, and he was not elected. Fame did not make Verlaine rich. He remained very poor. Some friends collected money for him every month, and he also received a small amount from the government. His health continued to become worse. Late in 1895, his bad leg became swollen again, and he grew very ill. Paul Verlaine died in Paris on 8 January 1896 from a disease of the lungs. He was 51 years old. A large crowd came to his funeral. Several well-known writers spoke beside the grave, including Mallarmé, Coppée, and Barrès. Verlaine was buried in the family grave at the Batignolles cemetery. Verlaine is best known as a poet of feelings and moods. He was very good at putting sad, gentle, and unclear feelings into words. He wrote about rain, autumn, evening, dreams, memory, love, and faith. He often showed how a feeling can grow or disappear without any clear cause. The best-known quality of Verlaine's poetry is its music. He chose his lines for their sound as well as for their meaning. He especially liked soft and gentle sounds. He often repeated similar sounds at the beginning or inside words. Because his poetry is so musical, many French composers, including Fauré and Debussy, used his poems for art songs written for a singer and piano. In his poem "Art poétique", written in prison in 1874 and later published in Jadis et Naguère, Verlaine asks poets to place music before everything else. Its most famous line is: This means "music before all things". Verlaine tells poets to choose soft and less exact words instead of hard and very clear ones. He prefers small differences of meaning to strong and bright colours. He even says that poets should "wring the neck" of grand and showy language. The poem is often read as a statement of Verlaine's own style. However, he later said that it was a song rather than a set of rules. He did not want all his poetry to be reduced to this single idea. Even so, its message about the sound of poetry had a strong influence on later poets. Verlaine's poems often seem easy to read. He liked plain, everyday words and tried to make his verse sound simple and natural, almost like ordinary speech. However, this simple sound came from careful work. There is great skill behind the easy surface. Critics often compare Verlaine to a painter and describe his poetry as "impressionist". His poems often catch one passing moment, a certain light, or a short-lived feeling instead of giving a fixed and complete picture. Some poems seem open or unfinished rather than neat and fully closed. Verlaine's poetry changed during his life. His early books, up to Romances sans paroles, are often seen as his most musical and delicate works. After prison, the religious poems in Sagesse became simpler and calmer. In his final books, his verse became even plainer. Many readers prefer his early poetry and believe that its music became weaker in the later works. Other critics disagree. They find new forms and fresh energy in some of his later books. Many of Verlaine's poems are short and easy to remember. Some of the best-known poems are described below. "Clair de lune" ("Moonlight") is the first poem in Fêtes galantes. It compares the soul of a loved person to a beautiful garden. People in fine clothes play music and dance there. They sing about love and good fortune, but they do not seem to believe their own happy words. A feeling of sadness can be heard beneath the music. "Chanson d'automne" ("Autumn Song"), from Poèmes saturniens, is one of the best-known poems in the French language. Its lines are very short and sound like sad music. The poem begins: This means "The long sobs of the violins of autumn". The poet says that these sounds fill his heart with pain. When the clock strikes, he remembers the past and begins to cry. At the end, he feels like a dead leaf carried away by a cruel wind. During the Second World War, radio messages using these lines helped to warn the French resistance that a large military attack was near. "Mon rêve familier" ("My Familiar Dream") is a sonnet, a poem of fourteen lines, from Poèmes saturniens. The poet says that he often has the same strange and moving dream. In it, he sees a woman whom he does not know. She loves and understands him. He cannot say whether her hair is dark, fair, or red. Her voice seems far away and calm, like the voices of loved people who have died. "Il pleure dans mon cœur" ("It Cries in My Heart"), from Romances sans paroles, places the rain falling on the town beside the sadness in the poet's heart. His heart is in pain, but he does not know why. Nobody has betrayed him, and he feels neither love nor hate. He says that the greatest pain is being sad without knowing the reason. Verlaine's work had a strong influence on the poets who came after him. His musical verse and his interest in soft and uncertain feelings strongly affected the Symbolist and Decadent poets of the late 19th century. His call for "music before all things" became a kind of motto for many of them. There is a strange point in this history. Young poets admired Verlaine most at a time when his own writing had already become simpler and plainer. Verlaine himself did not care much for these new movements. He said that when he suffered or cried, it was not a "symbol" but a real feeling. By the 1890s, many of the youngest poets had begun to move away from him. By then, however, he no longer needed their support. Verlaine also helped other poets in a direct way. In Les Poètes maudits, he wrote about writers who were little known at the time. Because of this book, more people began to read Rimbaud, Mallarmé, and Corbière. The story of Verlaine and Rimbaud is one of the best-known stories in French poetry, and the two men are often discussed together. Their love affair, their travels, and the shooting in Brussels have been described in many books, plays, and films. For a long time, some writers tried to hide or soften the truth about their relationship. Today, it is discussed openly. After Verlaine's death, some of his friends created a gentle and kindly picture of him as "poor good Verlaine". His difficult life, his years in prison, and his sad death also became part of his fame. In time, he came to be seen as one of the great poets of France. His poems are now taught in schools and studied at universities. Streets in French towns have also been named after him. Verlaine's poems have continued to live through music. His verse is easy to sing, so many musicians have set his poems to music. Well-known composers have written songs based on poems such as "Clair de lune". Because of this, many people who have never read his books still know some of his words. Les Poètes maudits (1884), essays about other poets Mémoires d'un veuf (Memoirs of a Widower, 1886) Confessions (1895), a book about his own life

Paul Valéry (30 October 1871 – 20 July 1945) was a French poet, essay writer, and thinker. His full name was Ambroise Paul Toussaint Jules Valéry. He is often regarded as one of the most important French writers of the early 20th century. Valéry wrote a small number of poems. Two works made him famous: the long poem La Jeune Parque (1917) and the book Charmes (1922), which contains his best-known poem, "Le Cimetière marin" ("The Graveyard by the Sea"). He also wrote a great deal of prose: essays, talks, and dialogues about art, science, the mind, and the state of Europe. Some of his best-known prose works are Monsieur Teste, Eupalinos, L'Âme et la Danse, and the collection Variété. For about fifty years Valéry also filled private notebooks, the Cahiers ("Notebooks"), almost every morning. He thought this was his real work. The notebooks were published in full only after his death, though a few small selections appeared during his lifetime. Valéry became one of the most honoured writers in France. He was elected to the Académie française and later became a professor at the Collège de France. When he died, the French government gave him a state funeral. Paul Valéry was born on 30 October 1871 in Sète, a port town in the south of France. At that time, the town's name was written as "Cette". His father, Barthélemy Valéry, worked for the customs service and came from Corsica. His mother, Fanny Grassi, came from Trieste. Throughout her life, she spoke Italian better than French. Both sides of the family had strong links with Italy and the sea. The port had a strong effect on Valéry throughout his life. He loved the sea, ships, and swimming, especially during summer visits to relatives in Genoa. Near the end of his life, he wrote that the gods of his childhood had been the sea, the sky, and the sun. For many years, he wanted to become an officer in the navy. However, he was not good enough at mathematics to enter the naval school, and he had to give up this first dream. Instead, he read many books. At first, he read Jules Verne and Victor Hugo. Later, he discovered Charles Baudelaire and other poets. He wrote his first poems in January 1884, when he was twelve years old. In the autumn of 1884, his family moved to Montpellier. Paul was bored at school and did not do well there. He later said that he had been a very poor pupil and that school had made him lose his knowledge of Greek and much of his Latin. He said that he later had to educate himself, like Robinson Crusoe alone on his island. Two interests from these years remained important throughout his life. In 1887, while he was in Genoa, he heard the opening music of Wagner's opera Lohengrin for the first time. He never forgot the experience. He also spent many hours in the town library, copying passages from large books about architecture. His early interest in the design of buildings appeared again many years later in his dialogue Eupalinos. On 14 March 1887, his father died suddenly. Paul was fifteen years old. After his death, the family almost never spoke about him again. One of Paul's school friends, Gustave Fourment, became his closest friend. Fourment was also the first person to read his poems and give him an honest opinion about them. In 1888, Valéry began to study law in Montpellier, mainly because his mother wanted him to do so. His first published poem appeared in a small magazine from Marseille in August 1889. In the same year, he read the novel À Rebours by Joris-Karl Huysmans. He also discovered the poetry of Stéphane Mallarmé and Arthur Rimbaud. Their works filled him with excitement, but also made him lose confidence. He felt that too many great modern works had already been written before he had begun to write. He then did one year of military service, which he hated. In May 1890, Valéry went to a student celebration by the sea near Montpellier. There he met Pierre Louÿs, a young writer from Paris. They soon discovered that they loved the same books, and they began to write to each other almost every day. Louÿs introduced him to André Gide, who visited Montpellier in December 1890. He also showed some of Valéry's poems to Mallarmé. In October 1890, Valéry wrote to Mallarmé himself. Mallarmé sent him a warm letter praising his work. Valéry remembered the letter so well that he could still repeat it from memory near the end of his life. In 1891, Louÿs published Valéry's poem "Narcisse parle" ("Narcissus Speaks") in his new magazine, La Conque. Valéry's name then began to become known among a small group of writers and readers. During these years, another student friend, Pierre Féline, taught him algebra and played Wagner's music for him on the piano. Valéry now began to love mathematics. He also read an essay in which Edgar Allan Poe explained how he had planned and written his poem "The Raven". Poe said that the poem had been made through careful thought, not through a sudden rush of feeling. This idea of writing through clear and careful thought remained important to Valéry throughout his life. In his first article, written when he was about eighteen, he already described the modern poet as "a cold scientist, almost an algebraist, in the service of a refined dreamer". A major change in his life came in October 1892, during the family's summer visit to Genoa. On the stormy night of 4 to 5 October, he stayed awake until morning. He later said that during this night "all his fate was being decided in his head". He decided to give up a secret love that could never succeed. He also decided to turn away, for the most part, from poetry. From then on, he wanted to serve only what he called "the Idol of the Intellect": the power of clear and controlled thought. This event became known as the "night of Genoa". It is often compared with the famous night in 1619 when the young René Descartes believed that he had discovered the main idea of his method. However, the story must be treated with care. Almost everything known about the night comes from Valéry's own accounts, written many years later. Scholars therefore believe that the story was partly a personal myth: a story about his own life that Valéry himself helped to create. On 3 March 1894, Valéry moved to Paris. He lived in a nearly empty room near the Jardin du Luxembourg, with a blackboard on the wall like a scientist. Every morning, he got up very early to work. He kept this habit for the rest of his life. In this room, he began the private notebooks that he called the Cahiers. He read many books about science, especially works by the mathematician Henri Poincaré. He hoped to discover the laws that control human thought. He planned a great book about the mind, which he called "the System", but he never wrote it. Valéry needed money. In 1896, he suddenly received an offer to go to London and translate articles for the company of Cecil Rhodes. The work lasted less than three weeks. Soon afterwards, an English review asked him to write an essay about the growth of German trade and power. The essay, later called Une conquête méthodique, was first published in January 1897 and was published again in French in 1915. It helped to make Valéry known as a careful writer about politics and events in the world. In 1897, he began work as a clerk in the Ministry of War. He found the work dull, but remained there for three years. During these years, Valéry wrote the two short prose works from his early career that are still best known. The Introduction à la méthode de Léonard de Vinci appeared in 1895. It had been written because someone had asked him for an article. It does not tell the story of Leonardo da Vinci's life. Instead, Valéry uses Leonardo to create a model of a mind able to understand and work in many different fields. La Soirée avec Monsieur Teste, published in 1896, presents Edmond Teste, a man who lives only for the powers of his own mind. His main question is: what can a man do? Many readers believed that Teste was a picture of Valéry himself. However, Mr Teste is not a simple portrait of the writer. He represents one part of Valéry's character, taken to its furthest possible point. Valéry added more pieces about him over many years, and the complete book Monsieur Teste appeared in 1926. Valéry's early political ideas were on the right. As a student, he went to lectures by Georges Vacher de Lapouge and helped him measure human skulls. Lapouge believed that human groups could be placed in a fixed order by race. These ideas are now known to be false and are regarded as pseudoscience, meaning ideas that claim to be scientific but do not follow good scientific methods. When the Dreyfus affair divided France at the end of the 1890s, Valéry supported the people who were against Alfred Dreyfus. He opposed a new trial and gave money to a fund for the widow of Colonel Henry, the officer who had made false evidence against Dreyfus. This choice has often been strongly criticized. Valéry later tried to explain his position, but his explanations did not end the criticism. Mallarmé was Valéry's highest example of what a poet could become, and he had great trust in the younger writer. In 1897, Valéry was among the first people allowed to read Mallarmé's last great poem, "Un coup de dés". Mallarmé died suddenly on 9 September 1898. Valéry said that he had lost the man he loved most in the world. A few months later, he entered a long period during which he published very little new work. On 31 May 1900, Valéry married Jeannie Gobillard, a niece of the painter Berthe Morisot. It was a double wedding. On the same day and in the same church, Jeannie's cousin Julie Manet married the painter Ernest Rouart. In 1902, Valéry and his wife moved to 40, rue de Villejust. The house had been built for Berthe Morisot. Valéry lived there for the rest of his life, and the street now bears his name. The couple had three children: Claude, born in 1903; Agathe, born in 1906; and François, born in 1916. Valéry made puppet shows for them and told them many stories. In July 1900, Valéry became the private secretary of Édouard Lebey, the head of the Havas news agency. Lebey was ill, so Valéry read newspapers to him and wrote his letters. He kept this job until Lebey died in 1922. For more than twenty years, Valéry published almost no new work. However, his mind was still very active. Every morning, he wrote in his Cahiers. He told Gide that he had chosen "a strategic life instead of a tactical one". He meant that he wished to save his strength for long years of thought instead of using it on many short pieces of writing. Valéry did not live alone like a hermit. Through his wife's family, he met many painters, and music remained very important to him. During the winter, he went to the famous Lamoureux concerts almost every Sunday. In 1901, a performance of Gluck's opera Orphée filled him with strong emotion. A well-known book of poetry published in 1900, Poètes d'aujourd'hui, also kept his early poems before the public. Around 1908, he went through a difficult period. He feared that his mind had become weaker and that he would never finish his planned "System". In 1912, Gide and the publisher Gaston Gallimard urged Valéry to collect his early poems in a book. He agreed without much pleasure and began to revise them. During this work, a new poem began to grow. At first, he planned a farewell poem of only thirty or forty lines. Over four years, it became the 512-line poem La Jeune Parque. When the First World War began, Valéry thought that he might have to join the army. He was not called up, but he felt useless while other men were fighting. He said that only the strict rules of classical verse allowed him to continue working at his desk. La Jeune Parque was published on 28 April 1917 in an edition of 600 copies and was dedicated to Gide. The critic Paul Souday wrote a long article about it. The article helped to make Valéry's name known again. Valéry then began to write more quickly. His poem "Le Cimetière marin" appeared in June 1920. Jacques Rivière took it to the printer while Valéry was still not sure that the poem was finished. The Album de vers anciens, published in 1920, brought together his revised early poems. Charmes, published in 1922, contained his newer poems. In 1921, a review asked its readers to name the seven greatest living French poets. Valéry came first. In his private notebook, he joked that he was neither great nor a poet. Valéry soon became famous. He went to the literary and artistic salons of Paris and became known as a brilliant speaker. His success had also been carefully prepared by important critics and by his friends. When Lebey died in 1922, Valéry lost his regular income. He now had to earn money from his writing. He gave public talks and wrote introductions, articles, and other pieces when people asked him to do so. In 1924, he helped to direct a new literary review called Commerce. The former follower of Mallarmé slowly became a kind of official poet of the Third Republic. In June 1920, Valéry met Catherine Pozzi, a highly educated writer who could read Greek easily. They began a deep but troubled relationship that lasted through most of the 1920s. It also left a mark on Valéry's poetry. In 1925, Valéry was elected to the Académie française, the old institution that studies and protects the French language. He took the seat that had belonged to Anatole France. When he was formally received into the Academy in 1927, he gave the usual speech in praise of the man who had held the seat before him. However, he did not once say Anatole France's name. Many people noticed this cold silence. His election came during a large public debate about "pure poetry", with Valéry's own poems at its centre. His fame had also spread beyond France. When he gave a talk in Berlin in 1926, the physicist Albert Einstein was among the people listening to him. During the 1930s, Valéry received many honours and took on many public duties. In 1929, the Academy gave him the difficult task of welcoming Marshal Philippe Pétain. Valéry gave the speech in January 1931. He looked back on the First World War and warned that Europe faced new dangers. He gave this warning two years before Adolf Hitler came to power in Germany. Valéry also wrote works for the stage with the composer Arthur Honegger. These were Amphion, first performed in 1931, and Sémiramis, first performed in 1934. Both works were first presented at the Paris Opera. Valéry was president of the French PEN Club from 1924 to 1934. Oxford University gave him an honorary degree in 1931. In 1932, he gave a speech about Goethe at the Sorbonne. The following year, he led the French group at a meeting of the League of Nations in Madrid. He also became head of the Mediterranean University Centre in Nice. In 1937, the Collège de France created a special chair of "poetics" for him. Poetics is the study of how poems and other works are made. The Collège de France is a famous institution in Paris where leading scholars give free courses open to the public. Valéry continued to teach there until the final months of his life. During his final years, Valéry loved Jeanne Loviton, a lawyer and writer who used the pen name Jean Voilier. He wrote many letters to her, but she often did not answer them. On Easter Sunday in 1945, she told him that she planned to marry the publisher Robert Denoël. Valéry then began to write in a green school notebook that he called Inferno. Day after day, he described the pain caused by losing her. France's defeat in 1940 was a great shock to Valéry. At first, Pétain's speech on the radio moved him deeply. However, he soon turned against the Vichy government. On 9 January 1941, he gave a speech in honour of the philosopher Henri Bergson, who had recently died. Bergson was Jewish, and the Vichy government had given him almost no official honour. Many people therefore understood Valéry's speech as an act of courage. Copies of it were secretly passed from person to person outside France. In 1941, the Vichy government removed Valéry from his position in Nice. However, he continued to teach at the Collège de France throughout the war. On 26 August 1944, after the liberation of Paris, he watched Charles de Gaulle and his soldiers move along the Champs-Élysées. Valéry then wrote a short and joyful piece called "Respirer" ("To Breathe"). In it, he said that freedom can be felt like fresh air. De Gaulle later invited him to dinner and told him that he would welcome his advice. Valéry was already weak from illness and refused the invitation. In May 1945, Valéry finished his last prose work, "L'Ange". It presents a pure mind looking at a human face in tears. He then began his last notebook with the Latin words Sub signo doloris, meaning "under the sign of pain". Valéry died in Paris on 20 July 1945, at the age of 73. The French government gave him a state funeral. On the night of 24 July, people carried his coffin by torchlight to the Palais de Chaillot. Lines written by Valéry can be seen on the walls of this building. De Gaulle led the official ceremony the following morning. Valéry was buried on 27 July in the graveyard by the sea in Sète. His poem "Le Cimetière marin" had made this graveyard famous. He was placed in the old tomb of his mother's family. Two years before his death, he had written a Latin sentence that would have been suitable for his grave: "I was a poet; now I have become poems." Valéry wrote only a small amount of poetry. The poems that he chose to keep fill about one hundred pages. He wrote most of them during two short periods of his life. La Jeune Parque (1917) is a long poem of 512 lines written in a classical form. A single woman speaks throughout the poem as she moves between sleep, sadness, and thought. It is often called one of the most difficult poems in French literature. However, the beauty of its language led many readers to believe that the poem had a hidden order. Valéry shaped it like a piece of music. He said that the sung speech in the operas of Gluck and the plays of Racine were his secret models. Valéry made more than one hundred drafts of the poem. About 450 sheets of paper still survive. They show fourteen different stages of the work. He wrote on many kinds of paper, sometimes on the backs of letters and bills. An early draft, published in 1951, shows him testing the words one by one. In the margin, he wrote a small list of words that he might use. Charmes (1922) contains twenty-one poems. Its title comes from the Latin word carmina, which means "songs". Valéry gave himself quiet tests of poetic skill. For example, he tried to write at least one poem in almost every traditional French line length. "La Pythie" gives a voice to the priestess of Delphi. Valéry dedicated it to Pierre Louÿs, in memory of their friendship and of Louÿs's love of Greece. In "Ébauche d'un serpent", the snake from the Garden of Eden speaks with anger and clever humour. The sound and mood of his voice keep changing. Valéry said that "Le Cimetière marin" began not with an idea, but with a poetic form. He wanted to write a long speech in a rarely used French line of ten syllables, with six lines in each stanza. The poem is set in the graveyard by the sea in Sète, above the port where Valéry was born. It is about time, death, and the desire to live. At the beginning of the poem are two lines in Greek by the ancient poet Pindar. They tell the soul not to seek life without end, but to do what is possible in the present world. One stanza speaks to Zeno of Elea, an ancient Greek thinker known for puzzles about movement. Valéry explained in 1945 that he had added this stanza late in the writing of the poem. He said that it helped to balance the whole work, like a small detail added by a painter to make a picture complete. The final lines contain Valéry's famous words: "The wind rises!... We must try to live!" These words later gave Hayao Miyazaki the title of his film The Wind Rises. The poem soon became a modern classic. In 1928, a scholar explained it line by line at the Sorbonne while Valéry himself was present. Rainer Maria Rilke also translated it into German. After Charmes, Valéry published almost no new poetry. Around 1937, people asked him to begin writing poems again. He answered that he had used up the vocabulary of Charmes. However, he continued to correct even his earliest poems. His sonnet "Naissance de Vénus" ("Birth of Venus") survives in at least three different forms, and he changed almost every line from one version to another. Today, many readers first discover Valéry through his prose. Gide believed that it was as good as his poetry, or perhaps even better. Valéry wrote several dialogues in the style of the ancient Greek writer Plato. In Eupalinos ou l'Architecte (1921), the dead Socrates and Phaedrus discuss buildings and art. Valéry wrote the work because a publisher had asked him to do so. It also had to fill an exact number of printed pages. Valéry enjoyed working under this strict rule. In L'Âme et la Danse (1921), Socrates and two friends watch a dancer and talk about the meaning of dance. L'Idée fixe (1932) is a quick and playful conversation between two modern men beside the sea. In the late Dialogue de l'arbre (1943), the Roman poet Lucretius and a shepherd talk in the shade of a large tree. At the request of a doctor, Valéry also translated Virgil's Bucolics into French verse. He worked on the translation between 1942 and 1944, but it was not published until 1953. To do the work, he opened again the old copy of Virgil that he had used at school. Valéry's essays and public talks about writers, art, and the modern world were collected in the five volumes of Variété, published between 1924 and 1944. His writings about political and world events appeared together in Regards sur le monde actuel (1931). He also wrote Degas Danse Dessin (1936), a book about the painter Degas, and collections of short thoughts such as Tel Quel. Valéry also wrote several works for the stage. These included the "melodramas" Amphion (1931) and Sémiramis (1934), with music by Honegger, and the Cantate du Narcisse (1938), with music by Germaine Tailleferre. In the ancient Greek story, the music of Amphion's lyre causes stones to rise by themselves and form walls. In Valéry's work, the stones build a temple. His last large project was Mon Faust ("My Faust"). He began it in 1940 to keep his mind active during a dark period. The work is formed from two connected plays: the comedy Lust and the more unusual drama Le Solitaire. Valéry planned them as parts of a "third Faust", following the two parts of the work by Goethe. However, he never completed the final acts. Le Solitaire was performed at the Comédie-Française on 17 April 1945, three months before Valéry died. There was one kind of book that Valéry refused to write: the novel. In 1924, André Breton reported a famous statement by him. Valéry said that he would always refuse to write a sentence such as "The marquise went out at five o'clock". He believed that, in this kind of prose, no detail was truly necessary. Almost anything could be changed without damaging the whole work. A poem, he said, is a closed system in which no part can be changed without affecting all the others. A novel is an open system, in which many details can be freely added, removed, or replaced. However, Valéry never completely gave up the idea of writing a different kind of novel. He imagined what he called "the novel of a brain", in which the only adventures would be movements of thought. The story of Monsieur Teste and many unfinished plans were part of this dream. The Cahiers ("Notebooks") were the work of Valéry's whole adult life. From 1894 until 1945, he filled about 260 notebooks, containing nearly 27,000 pages. Almost every morning, usually between five and eight o'clock, he sat down with coffee and a cigarette and wrote his thoughts. Valéry wrote the notebooks for himself, not for other readers. He often said that his published works were "applications" of ideas first developed in the Cahiers. The notebooks are not a diary, since Valéry laughed at that kind of writing. Instead, they contain many short notes, drawings, and, in later years, watercolour paintings. Their main subject is the human mind, but they also examine dreams, time, language, science, and art. In his later years, Valéry allowed small groups of notes to be published in books such as Cahier B 1910 and Rhumbs. These texts were later collected in Tel Quel. The complete Cahiers were published only after Valéry's death. With the help of his widow, the notebooks were first copied onto microfilm so that they would be kept safe. The French national research organisation, the CNRS, then published the whole collection in facsimile. This means that the books showed photographs of Valéry's original handwritten pages. Twenty-nine large volumes began to appear in 1957, with a preface by the physicist Louis de Broglie. The scholar Judith Robinson-Valéry later prepared a shorter selection in which the notes were placed in a clearer order. The notebooks have been called "a biography of the mind". Valéry did not wish to tell the story of his daily life. Instead, he tried to make a map of the way his mind worked. Valéry's main subject was the human mind. He wanted to understand how thought works in general. He studied its links with feelings, memory, and the body, and asked what words such as "self" and "attention" really mean. He saw the mind as a system that is always changing. He gave this idea a name of his own, "self-variance": for him, the most basic fact about the mind was its power to change. He also wrote many pages about sleep and dreams. Instead of asking what a dream means, he asked how a dream is made and how it works. He remained doubtful about the method of Sigmund Freud until the end of his life. Common words such as "will", "memory", and "time" seemed too unclear to him. He wanted to create a more exact language for the study of the mind, like the signs used in mathematics. Questions about language appear in the earliest pages of the Cahiers. Valéry was already thinking about them before the famous lectures of the Swiss scholar of language Ferdinand de Saussure were published in 1916. Later scholars have therefore seen Valéry as an early thinker about language. Valéry loved science throughout his life. He read many works by physicists and mathematicians. When he wrote about the mind and art, he often used images taken from stars, atoms, machines, and living things. He also knew several important scientists personally. He visited the laboratory of Marie Curie and spoke with Einstein, Jean Perrin, and Louis de Broglie. Valéry did not call himself a philosopher, and he often made fun of philosophy. However, many philosophers have studied his ideas seriously. Some scholars have placed him in an older French tradition of clear and careful thought. He admired Henri Bergson, although the two men thought in very different ways. He also read Nietzsche with great energy, describing himself as a "reader of prey". Valéry said that throughout his life he had trusted only his pure Self. By this, he meant the basic power of the mind to step back from every thought, feeling, or experience and observe it. He liked to compare this pure Self to the number zero in mathematics. He had left the Catholic faith of his childhood, but religion continued to interest him. A careful study published in 1944, which Valéry welcomed in a friendly letter, argued that his work was guided by a kind of faith centred on the self. This meant a belief in the mind and in its powers, but without belief in God. Valéry thought deeply about how poems are made. He did not believe that a poet should simply wait for a sudden feeling or a moment of inspiration. Careful work and clear thought were just as important. He strongly rejected the old idea that a god or a muse gives a complete poem to a poet who only has to write it down. However, as he grew older, he accepted that smaller forms of inspiration could exist. One of his favourite ideas was that inspiration is mainly a gift made by the reader. When readers are moved by a poem, they imagine that the poet must have been in an extraordinary state while writing it. Valéry also made a difference between lines that are "given" and lines that must be "made". He wrote that the gods kindly give the poet a first line for nothing. The poet's real task is then to make the following lines good enough to stand beside it. For Valéry, the sound of words was as important as their meaning, and a poem should work in a way similar to music. He explained this idea with the image of the Phoenix, the legendary bird that is born again from its own ashes. Ordinary language disappears once its meaning has been understood. A poem, however, must not be completely changed into a simple idea. Some difficulty or darkness should remain, so that the reader returns to the words, letters, and sounds of the poem. The human voice was at the centre of Valéry's art. He placed himself among writers who hear their work in their minds rather than see it. He also liked to repeat a lesson that came from the painter Degas: poems are made not with ideas, but with words. Valéry wrote about all the arts from the same point of view. He was mainly interested in the work, skill, and choices of the artist. A work of art should be carefully built, like a fine building. Dance seemed to him to be a form of thought expressed through movement. In a late note, he wrote that a work of art means "changing something in order to change someone". Valéry was therefore not only the cold thinker that he was sometimes said to be. His writing is full of the sea, trees, wind, and the light of morning. One of his main subjects was the meeting between the human mind and the natural world. After the First World War, Valéry wrote a famous essay called "La Crise de l'esprit" ("The Crisis of the Mind", 1919). Its opening sentence became one of the most often quoted lines of the century. Valéry wrote that civilisations, like human beings, can die. In the essay, Europe appears as a modern Hamlet, standing on a very large terrace and looking at millions of ghosts. Valéry saw Europe as one shared culture that must not break apart. He looked for ways to protect the life of the mind during a hard and dangerous period. One main question appears again and again in his essays: how does the growing human power over nature and technology change human beings themselves? He liked to imagine the great thinkers of the past standing before an electric generator, or dynamo, and being unable to understand it. Ancient Greece had a special place in Valéry's idea of Europe. Greek names appear throughout his work, from Narcissus and the Pythia to Socrates and Eupalinos. However, Valéry always said that he was not a scholar of ancient Greece. He read Greek writers in translation, and he never visited the country. He wrote that real contact with Greece would destroy his "Greece of crystal", the beautiful but false picture of Greece that he had made in his own mind. In a talk given in 1932, "Hellas et Nous" ("Greece and Us"), Valéry said in effect that every European is Greek without knowing it. For him, the deepest link between ancient Greece and modern Europe was the sea itself. A bright sea, seen from the shore, seemed to offer the mind the main qualities of knowledge: clearness, depth, great size, and measure. Valéry believed that the Mediterranean Sea had shaped the minds of the ancient Greeks in the same way that it had shaped his own childhood. When Valéry died, his fame seemed sure. Today his poetry is less widely read than it was in the 1920s and 1930s, and "Le Cimetière marin" remains his best-known poem. The rise of Surrealism turned taste toward a very different kind of poetry. The turn is striking, because the young leaders of Surrealism had first looked up to him: in 1919 Breton and Philippe Soupault asked his advice on a name for their new review, Littérature. His prose and his Cahiers, though, continue to interest many readers and scholars, and later writers were influenced by his ideas. In the 1960s a new group of French critics found him modern again, not so much as a poet as a thinker about literature. Gérard Genette wrote that almost all of Valéry's work reads like a long postscript, written after a very serious decision to stop writing. The publication of the Cahiers changed the picture most of all. At a ten-day meeting of scholars in 1965 they were presented as a body of work of a kind never seen before. A conference for the centenary of his birth, in 1971, was called "Paul Valéry Our Contemporary". His mark crossed borders early. The first English book on him appeared in London in 1933; later, T. S. Eliot honoured him above all as a poet, while Emil Cioran praised only the sharp observer of a tired civilisation. Poets of the Spanish "Generation of 1927" read and translated him. In Argentina, Jorge Luis Borges wrote, when Valéry died, that for his generation Valéry simply was Edmond Teste. In 1989 Benoît Peeters published an important modern biography, Paul Valéry, une vie d'écrivain ?. It asks how far Valéry staged his own legend, and calls him perhaps the greatest of the "writers without an œuvre": writers who never complete one single body of work. A university in Montpellier, the city of his student years, carries his name today. Album de vers anciens (1920) – early poems Le Cimetière marin (1920; also in Charmes) Introduction à la méthode de Léonard de Vinci (1895) La Soirée avec Monsieur Teste (1896); Monsieur Teste (1926) Variété I–V (1924–1944) – essays and talks Regards sur le monde actuel (1931) – on world events Degas Danse Dessin (1936) – on the painter Degas Dialogue de l'arbre (1943) – a late dialogue Amphion (1931) – first staged at the Paris Opera Sémiramis (1934) – first staged at the Paris Opera Cantate du Narcisse (written 1938; performed 1944) Mon Faust (two unfinished plays, Lust and Le Solitaire; book edition 1945–1946) Cahiers ("Notebooks", 1894–1945; printed after his death)

Paul the Apostle, (born as Saul of Tarsus) and also often called Saint Paul (2BC–64/65), was a Messianic Jewish-Roman writer and rabbi. He was a convert to Christianity. It is believed that he wrote thirteen books of the Bible, together called the Pauline epistles. They are letters to Christian churches and Christians. He wrote these letters to encourage them, to help them receive salvation, understand Christian teaching, and live Christian lives. Paul's name was originally Saul (not to be confused with King Saul from the books of Samuel in the Old Testament whom he was likely named after). Like the one he was named after, he was from the Tribe of Benjamin He grew up learning both the Jewish law and the Greek ways of discussing things. We are first introduced to Saul in the Bible near the end of Acts 7. The Christian movement had begun with the resurrection and ascension of Jesus. Saul was strongly against this, and he was happy as he watched Saint Stephen, the first martyr of Jesus, being killed by stoning after giving a speech that made the Jewish court angry. He worked for the Jewish High Priest and helped lead the arrests and killing of many Christians in Israel and the nearby area. Later on, Saul was told to go to Damascus to find and bring back Christians there to be punished. On the way, God came down from heaven and spoke to Saul. The Bible tells of what happened like this: When Saul reached Damascus, he was visited by Ananias (who was told by God to go pray for Saul), one of Jesus's disciples, where he got his sight back and was baptized as a Christian. He spent the next three years studying the Jewish scriptures again to find explanations for the Christian teachings. His experiences changed his view on Christianity completely. In Acts 13:9, he begins to be called Paul. This was the Hellenized version of the name Saul. He used his earlier education to explain his new faith to other people and to discuss things with people who had other beliefs. He travelled around the Roman Empire, teaching others about Christianity, and wrote letters back and forth with the churches he helped to begin. The letters contain many important parts of Christian teaching and have since been part of the New Testament of the Bible, coming between the Acts of the Apostles and the General Epistles. It is not known whether Paul actually wrote all of these letters, or whether other people could have helped write the letters. In some of them he refers to a co-author. In Catholic Churches parts of these letters are read at Mass as the second of two readings that come before the Gospel. Protestant Christians also use Paul's writings, especially the letter to the Romans to teach their ideas of Christian truth. Although the Bible does not say how Paul died, various writers said Paul was put to death by orders of the emperor Nero in Rome, in 64/65 AD. He had the rights of Roman citizenship, which meant that he could be put to death by beheading with a sword, rather than by crucifixion. Some stories say he was decapitated.

Paul Ludwig Hans Anton von Beneckendorff und von Hindenburg (2 October 1847 – 2 August 1934) was a German field marshal and statesman. Hindenburg retired from the army in 1911. He rejoined the German army at the start of the First World War. He became famous when he won the Battle of Tannenberg in 1914. Hindenburg retired again in 1919, but returned to public life one more time in 1925 to be elected as the second President of Germany. He was 84 years old and in poor health, but decided to run for re-election in 1932 as the only candidate who could defeat Adolf Hitler, because he saw him as a dangerous extremist. He tried to stop Hitler's and the Nazi Party's rise to power, but Franz von Papen persuaded Hindenburg, that the conservative elite and the military could control Hitler when he becomes Chancellor of Germany and that the other more dangerous alternative was communist rule. As a result, Hindenburg appointed Hitler as Chancellor on 30 January 1933. But von Papen's belief in controlling Hitler and his assurances to Hindenburg did not happen, because Hitler started to control them and gain more power. In March he signed the Enabling Act of 1933 which gave special powers to Hitler and his government. With this act, Hitler became a dictator in the next months, and crushed all opposition and banned all political parties, except the Nazi Party by the summer of 1933. Hindenburg died the next year, after which Hitler declared the office of President vacant and made himself Führer (Head of State and Head of Government) of Germany. The famous zeppelin Hindenburg that was destroyed by fire in 1937 had been named in his honour, as is the causeway joining the island of Sylt to mainland Schleswig-Holstein, the Hindenburgdamm, built during his time in office. In 1925, Hindenburg had no interest in running for public office. After the first round Admiral Alfred von Tirpitz, one of the leaders of the DNVP, visited Hindenburg and asked him to run. Hindenburg eventually agreed to run in the second round of the elections as a non-party independent, although he was a conservative. Because he was Germany's greatest war hero, Hindenburg won the election in the second round of voting held on 26 April 1925. He was helped when the Bavarian People's Party (BVP), switched its support from Marx, the SPD candidate and the Communist Party of Germany (KPD) to did not withdraw its candidate, Ernst Thälmann. If they had their supporters would most likely have voted for the SPD and Hindenburg may not have won. Hindenburg tried to stay out of day-to-politics, and be a ceremonial president. Even though he was a monarchist and wanted the restoration of the Hohenzollern dynasty (but not the other German dynasties), he took his oath to the Weimar Constitution seriously. Hindenburg often complained that he missed the quiet of his retirement and, that politics was full of ideas like economics that he did not understand. His advisers included his son, Oskar, his old army aide General Wilhelm Groener, and General Kurt von Schleicher. The younger Hindenburg served as his father's aide-de-camp and controlled politicians' access to the President. Schleicher came up with the idea of Presidential government, and the "25/48/53 formula". Under a "Presidential" government the chancellor is responsible to the president), and not the Reichstag. The "25/48/53 formula" was the three articles of the Constitution that could make a "Presidential government" possible: Article 25 allowed the President to dissolve the Reichstag. Article 48 allowed the President to sign into law emergency bills without the consent of the Reichstag. (The Reichstag could cancel any law passed by Article 48 by a simple majority within sixty days of its signing). Article 53 allowed the President to appoint the Chancellor. Schleicher's wanted to have Hindenburg appoint a chancellor that Schleicher chose. If that chancellor needed any laws he could use article 48. If the Reichstag should threaten to cancel any of those laws, Hindenburg could threaten a dissolution, and call new elections. Hindenburg did not like the idea, but was pressured into going along with them by his son and his other advisors. The first try at "presidential government" in 1926–1927 failed for lack of political support. During the winter of 1929–1930, Schleicher had a series of secret meetings with Heinrich Brüning, the leader of the Catholic Center Party (Zentrum). Schleicher then set about splitting the "Grand Coalition" government of the Social Democrats and the German People’s Party. As a result, the government fell in March 1930 and Brüning was named Chancellor by Hindenburg. Brüning's first act was to introduce a budget calling for steep spending cuts and sharp tax increases. When the budget was defeated in July, Brüning had Hindenburg sign the budget as an emergency law under Article 48. When the Reichstag voted to cancel the budget, Brüning had Hindenburg dissolve Reichstag only two years into its mandate, and had the budget passed again by Article 48. The Nazis got 17% of the vote in the September 1930 elections. The Communist Party of Germany also made gains. Brüning ruled through Article 48; the Social Democrats never voted not to cancel his Article 48 bills in order not to have another election that could only benefit the Nazis and the Communists. In the first round of the election held in March 1932, Hindenburg was the frontrunner, but did not have an absolute majority. In the runoff election of April 1932, Hindenburg beat Hitler for the Presidency. After the presidential elections had ended, Schleicher held a series of secret meetings with Hitler in May 1932, and thought that Hitler had agreed to support the new "presidential government" Schleicher was building. In May 1932 Schleicher had Hindenburg sack Groener as Defence Minister to humiliate both Groener and Brüning. On 31 May 1932, Hindenburg sacked Brüning as Chancellor and replaced him with Schleicher's suggestion, Franz von Papen. von Papen's government openly wanted to destroy German democracy. Like Brüning's government, von Papen's government was a "presidential government" that governed through the use of Article 48. As Schleicher wanted, Hindenburg dissolved the Reichstag and set new elections for July 1932. Schleicher and von Papen both believed that the Nazis would win the majority of the seats and would support von Papen's government. The Nazi party did become the largest party in the Reichstag, and expected Hitler would be Chancellor. When Hindenburg met Hitler on 13 August 1932, in Berlin, Hindenburg rejected Hitler's demands for the Chancellorship. The minutes of the meeting were kept by Otto Meißner, the Chief of the Presidential Chancellery. According to the minutes: Hindenburg issued a press release about his meeting with Hitler that seemed to say that Hitler had demanded absolute power and that the President had refused. Hitler was enraged by this press release. When the Reichstag met in September 1932, its first and only act was to pass a massive vote of no-confidence in von Papen’s government. In response, von Papen had Hindenburg dissolve the Reichstag for elections in November 1932. In the 1949 constitution, a vote of no confidence must be accompanied by the election of a new chancellor, so this could not happen. In the second Reichstag elections of 1932 the Nazis lost some support, but stayed the largest party in the Reichstag. There ensued another round of talks between Hindenburg, von Papen, von Schleicher on the one hand and Hitler and the other Nazi leaders on the other. Hitler still demanded that Hindenburg give him the Chancellorship. Hindenburg could not accept this, so von Papen suggested Hindenburg declare martial law and do away with democracy. Von Papen got Oscar Hindenburg to support the plan, and they persuaded the president to ignore his oath to the Constitution and go along with this plan. Schleicher saw von Papen as a threat so he blocked the martial law plan by saying it would make the Nazi SA and the Communist Red Front Fighters rebel, and that the Poles would invade and the Reichswehr would be unable to cope. Hindenburg hated the idea of Hitler as Chancellor, but under pressure from Meißner, von Papen and Oskar Hindenburg the President decided to appoint Hitler Chancellor. On the morning of 30 January 1933, Hindenburg swore Hitler in as Chancellor at the Presidential Palace. Hindenburg played key role in the Nazi Machtergreifung (Seizure of Power) in 1933. He was not involved in the planning, but did not stop Hitler. In the "Government of National Concentration" headed by Hitler, the Nazis were in the minority. Most of the ministers were from the von Papen and von Schleicher governments. Besides Hitler, the only other Nazi ministers were Hermann Göring and Wilhelm Frick. Hindenburg thought that the Nazis' power was limited, especially as his favourite politician, von Papen, was the Vice-Chancellor and the Reich Commissioner for Prussia. Hitler's first act as Chancellor was to ask Hindenburg to dissolve the Reichstag so that the Nazis and D.N.V.P. could increase their number of seats, Hindenburg agreed. In early February 1933, von Papen had an Article 48 bill signed into law that limited the freedom of press. After the Reichstag fire, Hindenburg signed into law the Reichstag Fire Decree. At the opening of the new Reichstag on 21 March 1933, at the Kroll Opera House, the Nazis staged an elaborate ceremony, in which Hindenburg played the leading part, that was meant to mark the continuity between the Prussian-German tradition and the new Nazi state. The ceremony at the Kroll Opera House had the effect of reassuring many Germans, especially conservative Germans, that life would be fine under the new regime. On 23 March 1933, Hindenburg signed the Enabling Act into law. Hindenburg was still very popular, but his health was getting worse. The Nazis made sure that whenever Hindenburg did appear in public Hitler was with him, and that Hitler was always very respectful to the President. The Nazi propagandists hoped people would think Hindenburg liked Hitler, and Hitler would become more popular, but privately Hitler and Hindenburg disliked and distrusted each other. The only time Hindenburg ever tried to stop a Nazi bill was in early April 1933. The Reichstag had passed a Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service. This said that all Jewish civil servants working for the Reich, the Länder, or the local districts should be sacked immediately. Hindenburg refused to sign this bill into law unless all Jewish veterans of World War I, Jewish civil servants who served in the civil service during the war and those Jewish civil servants whose fathers were veterans were allowed to stay in office. Hitler agreed, in order to get the law signed, even though he believed that the Jews had tried to undermine Germany during the Great War. It was Hindenburg who said that Germany lost the First World War because of politicians and others "stabbing the Army in the back". Hindenburg did not believe the story. He said it so that his wartime deputy Erich von Ludendorff would not write bad things in his memoirs. But Hitler did believe the story, and used it to gain power. Hindenburg stayed president until he died from lung cancer at his home in Neudeck, East Prussia on 2 August 1934. One day before Hindenburg's death, Hitler flew to Neudeck and visited him. Hindenburg, old and senile, thought he was meeting Kaiser Wilhelm II, and called Hitler "Your Majesty". He would be Germany's last president until 1945, when Karl Dönitz was appointed president in Hitler's last will. Following Hindenburg's death, Hitler declared the office of President to be permanently vacant, effectively merging it with the office of Chancellor under the title of Leader and Chancellor (Führer und Reichskanzler), making himself Germany's Head of State and Head of government. Hindenburg was buried in the Tannenberg Memorial near Tannenberg, East Prussia (today: Stębark, Poland). But Hindenburg always said he wanted to be buried next to his wife, whose body was taken from the cemetery and buried beside him in the Tannenberg Memorial. In 1945, German troops removed his and his wife's coffins, to save them from the approaching Soviet troops, and blew up the memorial with explosives. They were transported to Speyer and were buried in the Speyer Cathedral.

Paul the Octopus (said to be hatched January 2008 at Weymouth, England– 26 October 2010) was an octopus living in a tank at a Sea Life Centre in Oberhausen, Germany. Paul became famous around the world for correctly "choosing" the winner of Germany's seven matches at the 2010 World Cup, as well as the final. During the divinations, Paul was show two boxes with a mussel inside them, for food. Each box had, on the outside, a flag of a football team. Paul would eat the mussel from the box with the flag of the winning team. He did this correctly in four of Germany's six Euro 2008 matches, and in all seven of their matches in the 2010 World Cup. He correctly chose a win for Spain against the Netherlands in the World Cup final. His predictions were 100% (8/8) right for the 2010 World Cup and 86% (12/14) correct overall. Paul was retired after the 2010 FIFA World Cup. It was at first said that Paul's career as an oracle began during the UEFA Euro 2008 tournament. In the lead-up to Germany's international football matches, Paul (or a similar octopus) was presented with two clear plastic boxes, each containing food: a mussel or an oyster. Each container was marked with the flag of a team, one the flag of Germany, and the other the flag of Germany's opponent. The box which Paul opened first (and ate the contents of) was judged to be the predicted winner of the game. Some people had doubt about the octopus' abilities. Under the thought that Paul had the same chances of choosing the winner or the loser of a match, and not considering the chance of a draw, he had a 1/2 chance of rightly choosing any single game and a 1/256 chance of rightly choosing eight in a row. On October 26 2010, Paul died of natural causes after being inactive for the last few days.

Paula Deen (born January 19, 1947) is an American celebrity chef and television host. She has published fourteen cookbooks. She was born in Albany, Georgia. On June 21, 2013, The Food Network announced they would not renew her contract because Deen used racist slurs.

Pavla "Paula" Gruden (14 February 1921 – 26 January 2014) was a Slovenian and Australian poet, translator and editor. Her best known works were Svobodni Razgovori (1982), Snubljenje duha (1994) and Ljubezen pod džakarando (2002). Her writings were in both English and her native Slovenian. She was a member of the Slovene Writers' Association. Gruden was born in Ljubljana, Kingdom of Yugoslavia (now Slovenia) during World War II. She was sent to Nazi Germany for forced labour. In 1948, she immigrated to Australia. Gruden died from natural causes on 26 January 2014 in Sydney, New South Wales. She was 92 years old. She was outlived by her son, Danny.

Paula Danziger (August 18, 1944 – July 8, 2004) was an American author of children's and young adult literature. Danziger was born in Washington, D.C. to Samuel and Carolyn Danziger. Though she struggled in school as a child, she attended Montclair State University in New Jersey and earned a degree in 1967. She was a middle school teacher in New Jersey from 1967-1978 while studying for a Master's degree. Her studies were interrupted when she was in a car crash, where a drunk driver hit her car, and she slammed her head against the front window which caused her to have brain damage. In 1978 she left teaching to write full-time. Although readers loved her books because of the humor, some critics called them superficial and generic. Others praised her work for tackling real-life issues. Danziger died in 2004 after complications from a heart attack. She was 59. Some of the awards Danziger's work received: The Cat Ate My Gymsuit. Delacorte, 1974. The Pistachio Prescription. Delacorte, 1978. Can You Sue Your Parents for Malpractice?. Delacorte, 1979. There's a Bat in Bunk Five. Delacorte, 1980. The Divorce Express.
